title: Line Renaud? Quelle idée!  (Line Renaud? What an Idea!)

segments.t: Andréa swore she would win Françoise back, then made a mess of three apology messages on her voicemail. Now Gabriel walks in with a solution of his own: at lunch he offered the part to Line Renaud, the much-loved singer of the music hall. Camille, the assistant, is in the room too. Here's the scene in French first; just catch what you can.
Oui, Gabriel? C'est quoi, ça?
Line Renaud pour remplacer Françoise Fabian.
Quelle idée! Line Renaud dans un film de Rajevski?
Génial, non?
Pourquoi pas Enrico Macias?
Line Renaud est belle, du bon âge, et très populaire.
Gabriel, tu as complètement perdu la tête!
J'aime bien Line Renaud, mais elle n'est pas faite pour ça.
Pas dans un film de Gabor!
Je ne vais pas m'humilier. Je sais qu'il dira non.
Ça pourrait sauver le film.
Ce serait un autre film.
Tu peux être tellement snob, Andréa. C'est pitoyable!
J'ai des convictions, c'est tout.
C'est qui, Line Renaud?
Let's go through it together. Gabriel proposes a replacement for Françoise, and Andréa immediately questions his choice.
Oui, Gabriel? C'est quoi, ça?
'Yes, Gabriel? What's that?' This second question is the casual, spoken way to ask 'what is that': literally 'it's what, that?'. In careful French the question word would come first.
Line Renaud pour remplacer Françoise Fabian.

'Line Renaud, to replace Françoise Fabian.' The name comes first, followed by the purpose: to replace the other actress. The short link before replace is the same one used for for; here it introduces what Gabriel wants Line to do.
Quelle idée!
'What an idea!' The word for 'what' here is an exclamation, and it agrees with the feminine word for 'idea'. From Andréa, it's not a compliment.
Line Renaud dans un film de Rajevski?
'Line Renaud in a Rajevski film?' The director's name follows of in French, where English can put Rajevski directly before film. Andréa repeats the proposed casting as a sceptical question.
Génial, non?
'Brilliant, isn't it?' The little word for 'no' at the end asks her to agree. Gabriel is very pleased with himself.
Pourquoi pas Enrico Macias?
'Why not Enrico Macias?' Why not can be a serious suggestion or an ironic challenge. Andréa names another popular singer to mock Gabriel's choice, rather than actually suggesting a new cast member.
Line Renaud est belle, du bon âge, et très populaire.
'Line Renaud is beautiful, the right age, and very popular.' Three good reasons. 'The right age' is literally 'of the good age'.
Gabriel, tu as complètement perdu la tête!
'Gabriel, you've completely lost your mind!' Literally 'you have completely lost the head'. This is the everyday past: the action word 'have', then the action.
J'aime bien Line Renaud, mais elle n'est pas faite pour ça.
'I like Line Renaud, but she's not made for this.' Adding the word for 'well' after the action word for 'love' softens it to 'I like'. And the word for 'made' is feminine, because it describes Line.
Pas dans un film de Gabor!
'Not in a Gabor film!' This is a shortened refusal: she leaves out the rest of I will not put her. The preposition in still links the actress with the production she supposedly does not suit.
Je ne vais pas m'humilier.
'I'm not going to humiliate myself.' The verb 'to go' plus another verb is the easy French future. Here it's negative, wrapped by the two little words for 'not'.
Je sais qu'il dira non.
'I know he'll say no.' This time it's the real future tense of the verb 'to say'.
Ça pourrait sauver le film.
'It could save the film.' Could presents a possible result, not a certainty. Save means prevent the project from collapsing here, rather than rescue someone from physical danger.
Ce serait un autre film.
'It would be a different film.' The same 'would' ending, on the verb 'to be'. For Andréa, art comes first.
Tu peux être tellement snob, Andréa.
'You can be such a snob, Andréa.' The French borrowed the English word for a snob. Gabriel, usually so gentle, is hurt.
C'est pitoyable!

'It's pathetic!' Pathetic is a strong criticism here, rather than a sympathetic word for someone deserving pity. The same spelling works for masculine and feminine descriptions. Gabriel thinks Andréa is being snobbish.
J'ai des convictions, c'est tout.
'I have convictions, that's all.' The last two words, 'that's all', are a handy way to close a discussion.
C'est qui, Line Renaud?

'Who's Line Renaud?' Camille is in her early twenties, and she has no idea who this legend is. The question word comes last here, which is very common in spoken French. Here's the whole argument once more, in French. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more.
Oui, Gabriel? C'est quoi, ça?
Line Renaud pour remplacer Françoise Fabian.
Quelle idée! Line Renaud dans un film de Rajevski?
Génial, non?
Pourquoi pas Enrico Macias?
Line Renaud est belle, du bon âge, et très populaire.
Gabriel, tu as complètement perdu la tête!
J'aime bien Line Renaud, mais elle n'est pas faite pour ça.
Pas dans un film de Gabor!
Je ne vais pas m'humilier. Je sais qu'il dira non.
Ça pourrait sauver le film.
Ce serait un autre film.
Tu peux être tellement snob, Andréa. C'est pitoyable!
J'ai des convictions, c'est tout.
C'est qui, Line Renaud?
Well done: that was a fast, funny row, and you followed it. Keep your ears open, because Gabriel is about to have doubts of his own. See you next time!
À plus tard!
